rules.citation: CT Public Health Code Reg. 19-13-B51d(a)(2)
rules.condition: Well with a required withdrawal rate under 10 gpm — the band a single-family home sits in.
rules.subject: Well to a system for disposal of sewage or other source of pollution
rules.buyer_sentence: 75 ft from septic and other pollution sources for a typical home well — the band follows the home’s required withdrawal rate (its water demand), not the well’s tested yield; the 150 ft band is for larger or shared supplies that must deliver 10–50 gpm, and 200 ft above 50 gpm.

rules.citation: CT DPH Technical Standards for Subsurface Sewage Disposal Systems, Table 1 Item A (applied to wells via Reg. 19-13-B102d)
rules.condition: Applies when BOTH hold: soil percolation rate faster than 1.0 minute per inch, AND the bottom of the leaching system is less than 8 ft above ledge rock. For a single-family home the 75 ft distance becomes 150 ft. Only soil tests on the lot can settle whether this applies — it cannot be screened from public data.
rules.subject: Well to leaching system distance DOUBLES when the soil is fast AND the ledge is shallow

rules.citation: CT Public Health Code Reg. 19-13-B51d (bands keyed to 'required withdrawal rate'); Reg. 19-13-B51b(18) defines 'yield' separately and B51d never uses it
rules.condition: ACCEPTED OPERATING ASSUMPTION (Marcin, 2026-10-16): a single-family home sits in the under-10 gpm band and gets the 75 ft distance, regardless of what its well tests at. A well's tested yield does not move it into a higher band. The code never prints a demand table for a house, so this rests on the standard professional reading (Summer Hill Civil Engineers' 2022 interpretation letter to DPH; no published DPH ruling found) — the OPINION label stays on it.
rules.subject: Which band governs: the required withdrawal rate is the water demand of what the well serves — NOT the well's tested yield

rules.citation: CT Public Health Code Reg. 19-13-B51d (lead-in and (a)(2))
rules.condition: B51d's text runs the distance to 'a system for disposal of sewage' — the leaching system, not the septic tank and not a center point. Whether the 100% reserve leaching area counts as part of 'the system' for this measurement is professional practice, not printed text (audit Q2 — open, labeled).
rules.subject: How distances are measured: horizontally, to the sewage disposal system itself

rules.citation: CT Public Health Code Reg. 19-13-B51m(b)
rules.condition: A well permit may not issue for a parcel whose boundary lies within 200 ft of an approved community public water supply, measured along a street, alley, or easement. This is why abandonment-heavy, public-water neighborhoods are a permit problem, not just a data gap.
rules.subject: No well permit when the parcel is within reach of an approved public water supply

rules.citation: CT Public Health Code Reg. 19-13-B51m(a)
rules.condition: The local director of health must be satisfied the lot has a feasible sewage disposal method before a well is permitted — in practice the septic question is decided first or alongside.
rules.subject: Well permits are gated on sewage feasibility

rules.citation: CT Public Health Code Reg. 19-13-B51m(c); CGS 19a-37(e) (regulations to clarify exception criteria)
rules.condition: The Commissioner of Public Health holds limited exception authority over the B51m permit restrictions.
rules.subject: Commissioner exceptions to the public-water permit bar

rules.condition: A person may apply to DPH for an exception to the separating-distance requirements for repair or new construction of a subsurface sewage disposal system relative to a water supply well. All owners of properties with wells affected must be notified by certified mail, return receipt requested, with a copy of the application. An approval is NOT an affirmative defense to contamination liability claims. This statute — not a general health-director discretion — is the real exception path.
rules.subject: DPH exceptions to separating distances for a sewage system near a well

rules.citation: RCSA 25-128-41 (effective 1978; amended 2022-07-08)
rules.condition: The location of any water supply well is subject to approval by the local health officer of the municipality, per CGS 19a-39 and Reg. 19-13-B51d.
rules.subject: Well location needs local health officer approval

rules.citation: CGS 19a-37(c)(2) (current text, read 2026-10-22); CT DPH Circular Letter 2022-60 (2022-10-05) — superseded on the lead/recipient points
rules.condition: Effective 2022-10-01, the owner of a newly constructed well must test for the statutory baseline panel (15 parameters); the statute says the test shall 'include, but need not be limited to' them, so the list is a floor, not a closed panel. Lead is NOT baseline: 'If such a well is constructed for an existing structure, a first draw sample collected from the existing plumbing system shall also be tested for lead.' Results go to the LOCAL health authority, which determines compliance with the MCLs (RCSA 19-13-B101/B102); the well may not be used for domestic purposes until it determines compliance. Corrected 2026-10-22 (Codex R17): the prior 16-count came from PA 22-58 as originally enacted / DPH Circular Letter 2022-60, which listed lead in the baseline and DPH as recipient; the current statutory text supersedes both points.

conditional_parameters.condition: well constructed for an existing structure — a first draw sample collected from the existing plumbing system must also be tested for lead

rules.subject: Required water testing for a newly constructed private or semipublic well: 15 baseline parameters, plus first-draw lead when the well serves an existing structure; the local health authority must determine MCL compliance before domestic use

rules.citation: CT Public Health Code Reg. 19-13-B51k; RCSA 25-128-51
rules.condition: Every new well must pass the code's yield test at a pumping rate at least equal to its required withdrawal rate (test durations scale by band: 4 / 36 / 72 hours). No provision of B51 sets a minimum yield a private home's well must produce. (A district may add a local minimum-yield table — Redding does; check the district layer.)
rules.subject: Yield testing is mandatory; there is no minimum gpm for a private home well in B51

rules.citation: CT DPH Technical Standards for Subsurface Sewage Disposal Systems, Table 1
rules.condition: Minimum 15 ft, reducible to 10 ft in defined situations. This constrains where the septic can go, which is what makes tight lots tight — it is not a distance the well must keep.
rules.subject: Leaching system to property line (septic-side rule — NOT a well setback)

rules.citation: CT DPH Technical Standards for Subsurface Sewage Disposal Systems, Table 1 / s.II.E
rules.condition: Every lot must hold a reserve leaching area equal to the primary system, kept available. Whether the well distance is measured to the reserve area as part of 'the system' is professional practice, not printed text (audit Q2 — open, labeled).
rules.subject: A 100% reserve leaching area is required and treated as part of the system

rules.citation: CT DPH Technical Standards for Subsurface Sewage Disposal Systems, Table 1 Item D
rules.condition: 100 ft from a leaching system to a public water-supply reservoir watershed; 50 ft to a private reservoir. Audit M5: this figure was previously misattributed in our materials as a well-to-reservoir setback. There is no well-to-reservoir distance in B51d.
rules.subject: Leaching system to a water-supply reservoir (septic-side rule — NOT a well setback)

rules.citation: files/rules-step0-research-2026-10-15.md (Q3)
rules.condition: Step-0 resolution (2026-10-15): no post-2006 amendment to 19-13-B51d was found in the Secretary of State Title 19 PDF (page-stamped 2-06), Cornell LII section notes, DPH circulars, or the 2022 regulation-making record. The 2022 changes (PR2020-017, effective 2022-07-08) amended the Well Drilling Code (RCSA 25-128-1 to 25-128-64), not B51d. One direct browse of the Title 19 section in the eRegulations portal is still owed — this is 'no amendment found', not proven-none.
rules.subject: Edition status of the B51d text encoded here

rules.citation: NCDHD Subdivision Plan Review Requirements, item 5 (Rev. 06/30/26)
rules.condition: NCDHD's subdivision plan-review requirements say no well should be located closer than 25 ft to a property boundary 'if possible'. It is published guidance in a plan-review document — present it as guidance the district will look for, never as a state setback, and note no B51d well-to-property-line distance exists.
rules.subject: Well to property boundary: 25 ft 'if possible' (district plan-review guidance, NOT a hard setback)

rules.citation: NCDHD Sanitary Code s.6.B(4)(b)
rules.condition: District sanitary code rule for irrigation wells only — landowners register the well and keep a 75 ft radius to property lines, or produce a recorded easement/release from every affected neighbor. Does not apply to drinking-water wells.
rules.subject: Irrigation wells: 75 ft radius from property lines unless the neighbor grants an easement

rules.buyer_sentence: About $25 per foot for drilling and casing when the geology cooperates.
rules.citation: CostHelper, 2026 Cost of Well Drilling (drilling, casing and cap $15-$30/ft); NGWA Well Owners Guide, 2017 (drilling-only averages about $24/ft for a 4-inch well, about $30/ft for a 6-inch well)
rules.condition: Low planning point for drilling and casing when the geology cooperates: shallow local depth, standard 6-inch bedrock well.
rules.scope: Drilling and casing. Excludes pump, pressure tank, electrical, trenching, and permit.
rules.subject: Drilled well cost per foot, drilling and casing, easy case

rules.buyer_sentence: About $45 per foot for drilling and casing is the plan-on number for a typical Connecticut bedrock well.
rules.citation: Planning point inside published ranges: CostHelper, 2026 Cost of Well Drilling (difficult ground $30-$50/ft or more); DrillerDB Northeast hard-rock band ($40-$75/ft); Angi, updated 2026-09-18 (depth table implies $35.50/ft for 4-inch PVC casing and $61.20/ft for 6-inch steel casing)
rules.condition: Mid planning point for drilling and casing at the local median depth in Connecticut bedrock. No source publishes $45 as a figure; it is a project planning point bounded by the cited ranges.
rules.scope: Drilling and casing. Excludes pump, pressure tank, electrical, trenching, and permit.
rules.subject: Drilled well cost per foot, drilling and casing, plan-on case

rules.buyer_sentence: About $65 per foot for drilling and casing when the hole runs deep or the rock fights you.
rules.citation: Angi, How Much Does Well Drilling Cost, updated 2026-09-18 (rocky, sloped, or remote terrain $50-$75/ft); DrillerDB Northeast hard-rock band ($40-$75/ft)
rules.condition: High planning point for drilling and casing when the hole runs deep or the rock fights: local maximum depth or town p90 depth.
rules.scope: Drilling and casing. Excludes pump, pressure tank, electrical, trenching, and permit.
rules.subject: Drilled well cost per foot, drilling and casing, hard case

rules.buyer_sentence: Carry a $10,000 to $25,000 contingency for a dry or low-yield hole. It is our planning allowance, not a published figure.
rules.citation: Project planning allowance. Basis: DrillerDB (drilling billed per foot whether or not the hole produces; a 300-ft dry hole at $4,500-$7,500 at drilling-only rates); HomeGuide (hydrofracturing $1,500-$3,000; redrilling deeper $3,000-$6,000); CT DPH report to the General Assembly, 2009-06-30 (low-yield bedrock areas exist statewide)
rules.condition: Allowance for a dry or low-yield first hole: the failed attempt is billed per foot, and recovery means hydrofracturing, deepening, or a second hole. No published source states this range; it is arithmetic on the cited rates at Connecticut depths of 200 to 400 feet.
rules.scope: Contingency on top of the drilling and casing band.
rules.subject: Dry-hole and low-yield contingency allowance
